lessonTitle: Shaft Design for Strength and Fatigue

blocks.text: A gearbox shaft can be perfectly strong enough to carry its torque and still fail the gearbox, because a shaft that bends too much tilts the gears so that the teeth mesh on one edge and the bearings run with their rollers skewed. A shaft must therefore be checked twice: once for strength and fatigue at its most stressed section, and again for stiffness.

blocks.markdown: A rotating shaft carries gears and pulleys that apply forces and torque. Resolve the forces into two perpendicular planes, find the bearing reactions, and draw the bending-moment diagram in each plane; the resultant moment $M$ at each section is the vector sum. Because the shaft rotates, a fixed bending moment produces a stress that reverses every revolution, so the **bending stress is fully reversed** (alternating), while a steady torque $T$ produces a **steady (mean) shear stress**. The critical sections are shoulders, keyways and grooves where $M$ or $T$ is large and the diameter is small.

blocks.title: Fatigue stress concentration factor
blocks.text: A geometric stress concentration factor $K_t$ (bending) or $K_{ts}$ (torsion) is the ratio of peak elastic stress at a feature to the nominal stress. In fatigue the full peak is not felt, because the material is notch-insensitive to some degree. The fatigue factor is $K_f=1+q(K_t-1)$, where $q$ in the range 0 to 1 is the notch sensitivity (and similarly $K_{fs}=1+q_s(K_{ts}-1)$ for torsion). It multiplies the nominal stress, and for ductile material in a mean stress it is applied only to the alternating component in the simplest treatment, but Shigley's DE-Goodman form below applies it to both.

blocks.caption: Typical first-iteration stress concentration factors for shafts (indicative, Shigley Table 7-1; refine when the dimensions are known)

blocks.markdown: **Sizing for fatigue.** For a rotating shaft with fully reversed bending moment $M_a$ and steady torque $T_m$ (so $M_m=T_a=0$), the distortion-energy (von Mises) combination with the Goodman line gives the factor of safety $n$ in terms of the diameter $d$. In SI units, with $M$ and $T$ in N mm and strengths in MPa, the relation and its inverse for the minimum diameter are shown below. The equations come from $\sigma_a'=\sqrt{\sigma_a^2+3\tau_a^2}$ and $\sigma_m'=\sqrt{\sigma_m^2+3\tau_m^2}$ with $\sigma=32M/(\pi d^3)$ and $\tau=16T/(\pi d^3)$, inserted in the Goodman equation $\sigma_a'/S_e+\sigma_m'/S_{ut}=1/n$.

blocks.caption: DE-Goodman criterion for a shaft with alternating bending and steady torque (Shigley, M and T in N mm, S in MPa gives d in mm)

blocks.title: Minimum diameter at a shoulder
blocks.prompt: A steel shaft ($S_{ut}=600$ MPa, corrected endurance limit $S_e=230$ MPa) has a shoulder where the alternating bending moment is 180 N m and the steady torque is 120 N m. The stress concentration at the fillet is $K_t=2.1$ in bending with notch sensitivity $q=0.8$, and $K_{ts}=1.7$ in torsion with $q_s=0.85$. Find the minimum diameter for $n=2.0$.

steps.text: Bracket terms in the DE-Goodman expression (N mm and MPa).
Sum and insert in the diameter equation.
Round up to a standard 35 mm and verify. The factor of safety for $d=35$ mm follows from the first equation.

blocks.answer: The minimum diameter is 32.9 mm; a 35 mm shaft gives n = 2.41. Note that the shoulder, not the plain shaft, controls the size.

blocks.markdown: **Deflection and slope.** A shaft must also be stiff enough. Excessive slope at a bearing misaligns the rolling elements or the oil film and shortens bearing life, and excessive transverse deflection or slope at a gear reduces tooth contact and increases noise and wear. The designer therefore calculates the deflection $y$ and slope $\theta$ from the beam equations, using the shaft's second moment of area $I=\pi d^4/64$ and the modulus $E$ (steel $E\approx207$ GPa), then compares them with limits. Typical guideline values (indicative; check the bearing and gear manufacturer): slope at a deep-groove ball bearing about 0.001 to 0.003 rad, at tapered or cylindrical roller bearings about 0.0005 to 0.0012 rad, and slope across a spur gear mesh about 0.0005 rad.

blocks.caption: Simply supported shaft of span L with a single load F at distance a from support A and b from support B (a + b = L); central load: y = FL^3/(48EI)

blocks.title: Deflection and slope check
blocks.prompt: A 35 mm diameter steel shaft ($E=207$ GPa) is simply supported over a 400 mm span and carries a gear load of 3.2 kN at 150 mm from bearing A. Find the deflection at the gear and the slopes at the two bearings.

steps.text: Deflection under the load with $a=150$ mm and $b=250$ mm.
Slope at the nearer bearing A.
Slope at the farther bearing B.

blocks.answer: Deflection at the gear is 0.25 mm; the slopes are 0.00213 rad at A and 0.00180 rad at B, which is acceptable for deep-groove ball bearings (up to about 0.003 rad, typical) but too large for roller bearings (about 0.0012 rad) and well above the guideline for a gear mesh, so the shaft would need stiffening or a different layout.

items: Stiffness scales with $d^4$ through $I$, so a 10 per cent increase in diameter reduces deflection by about 32 per cent.
Deflection depends on $E$, which is nearly the same for all steels, so changing to a stronger steel does not help stiffness.
Shorten the span, place bearings close to the gears, or add a bearing to cut deflection.
Use generous shoulder fillets, relief grooves and gently rounded keyways to reduce $K_f$.

blocks.title: Strength first, then stiffness
blocks.text: Estimate the diameter from fatigue at the critical section including $K_f$ and $K_{fs}$, round up to a standard size, then check deflection and slope. In practice the stiffness check often governs the final diameter for long, heavily loaded shafts, and the fatigue check governs for short ones.

points: A rotating shaft sees fully reversed bending and usually steady torque, so the fatigue analysis uses $M_a$ and $T_m$ with the DE-Goodman criterion.
Stress concentration enters through $K_f=1+q(K_t-1)$ and $K_{fs}$; shoulders, keyways and grooves are the critical features.
Check deflection and slope with beam equations ($I=\pi d^4/64$) against limits for bearings and gear meshes; stiffness scales with $d^4$.

questions.stem: A shaft rotates at constant speed under a bending moment that is fixed in direction. How does the bending stress at a point on the surface vary with time?

options.text: It is fully reversed, going from tension to compression once per revolution
It is zero except at the bearings

questions.correctOptionText: It is fully reversed, going from tension to compression once per revolution

distractorRationale.a: Correct: a surface point rotates from the tension side to the compression side and back.
distractorRationale.b: The point passes through the compression side too.
distractorRationale.c: The surface alternates, so it is not steady.
distractorRationale.d: The stress is non-zero in the loaded span.

questions.explanation: A point on the surface sits on the tension side for half a revolution and on the compression side for the other half. The bending stress is therefore alternating with zero mean, while a steady torque gives a steady shear stress.

questions.stem: A shoulder has a theoretical stress concentration factor $K_t=2.5$ and a notch sensitivity $q=0.8$. What is the fatigue stress concentration factor $K_f$?

distractorRationale.d: 1.8 subtracts 0.7 from K_t, which has no basis.

questions.explanation: $K_f=1+q(K_t-1)=1+0.8\times1.5=2.2$. The fatigue factor lies between 1 (no notch effect) and $K_t$ (full effect) depending on notch sensitivity.

questions.stem: Which change at a shaft shoulder most directly reduces the stress concentration there?

options.text: Reducing the fillet radius to save space
Cutting a keyway across the shoulder

distractorRationale.a: Correct: a larger radius makes the flow of stress smoother.
distractorRationale.b: A sharp corner raises Kt to about 2.7 or more.
distractorRationale.c: Roughness adds to the surface-finish penalty.
distractorRationale.d: A keyway adds a stress raiser.

questions.explanation: A generous fillet radius reduces $K_t$ from about 2.7 (sharp) to about 1.7 (well rounded). The same idea applies to relief grooves and to the ends of keyways.

questions.stem: A steel shaft is found to deflect too much. The diameter is increased by 10 per cent. By approximately what factor does the deflection under the same load fall?

options.text: It becomes about 0.68 of its previous value
It becomes about 0.91 of its previous value
It becomes about 0.83 of its previous value

questions.correctOptionText: It becomes about 0.68 of its previous value

distractorRationale.a: Correct: deflection varies as 1/I, proportional to d^-4: 1/1.1^4 = 0.683.
distractorRationale.b: 0.91 assumes deflection inversely proportional to d.

questions.explanation: The second moment of area is $I=\pi d^4/64$, so deflection varies as $d^{-4}$. A 10 per cent larger diameter gives $1/1.1^4=0.68$ of the deflection, a 32 per cent reduction.

questions.stem: Why is the slope of the shaft at a bearing limited in design?

options.text: Excess slope misaligns the rolling elements or the oil film, causing edge loading and shortening bearing life
Slope has no effect on bearings but affects the key
Slope increases the shaft's endurance limit

questions.correctOptionText: Excess slope misaligns the rolling elements or the oil film, causing edge loading and shortening bearing life

distractorRationale.a: Correct: bearings are designed for a nearly parallel shaft.
distractorRationale.c: The bearing is the first component affected.
distractorRationale.d: Slope does not alter the endurance limit.

questions.explanation: A tilted shaft loads one edge of a roller or the end of a plain bearing, causing high local stresses and rapid wear. Limits depend on the bearing type, with self-aligning bearings accepting much more tilt.

questions.stem: A shoulder fillet has a stress concentration factor $K_t=2.3$ and the material notch sensitivity is $q=0.85$. Find the fatigue stress concentration factor $K_f$ (dimensionless).
questions.explanation: Using $K_f=1+q(K_t-1)=1+0.85\times1.3=2.105$. The fatigue effect is therefore a little less than the full theoretical concentration of 2.3.

questions.stem: A solid steel shaft of diameter 30 mm ($E=207$ GPa) is simply supported over a span of 500 mm and carries a single load of 2.5 kN at mid-span. Find the mid-span deflection in mm.
questions.explanation: The second moment of area is $I=\pi\times30^4/64=39761$ mm$^4$. Then $y=FL^3/(48EI)=2500\times500^3/(48\times207000\times39761)=0.791$ mm.

questions.stem: A 35 mm diameter shaft carries a fully reversed bending moment of 150 N m and a steady torque of 100 N m at a section where $K_f=1.8$ and $K_{fs}=1.5$. The strengths are $S_e=200$ MPa and $S_{ut}=550$ MPa. Using the DE-Goodman relation for a rotating shaft, find the factor of safety (dimensionless).
questions.explanation: In N mm and MPa, $2K_fM_a/S_e=2\times1.8\times150000/200=2700$ and $\sqrt3K_{fs}T_m/S_{ut}=\sqrt3\times1.5\times100000/550=472.4$, so the bracket is 3172. Then $1/n=16\times3172/(\pi\times35^3)=0.3768$ and $n=2.65$.

questions.stem: Outline the procedure for finding the minimum diameter of a stepped shaft at a shoulder for a given fatigue factor of safety, listing the data you need and explaining why the process is iterative.
markingGuide: Draw free-body diagrams in two planes, find reactions, bending-moment and torque diagrams, and the resultant alternating moment $M_a$ and steady torque $T_m$ at the shoulder.
Material data: $S_{ut}$, $S_y$ and the corrected endurance limit $S_e$ from the Marin factors.
Stress concentration: $K_t$, $K_{ts}$ from the geometry and $K_f=1+q(K_t-1)$, $K_{fs}$ with notch sensitivities.
Apply DE-Goodman, $d=\{(16n/\pi)[2K_fM_a/S_e+\sqrt3K_{fs}T_m/S_{ut}]\}^{1/3}$ to find the minimum diameter, and round to a standard size.

Iterative because $S_e$ (size factor $k_b$), $K_t$ (depends on $r/d$ and $D/d$) and $q$ (depends on $r$) depend on the diameter being found, so estimate, compute, update and repeat; check yield and deflection after.
questions.explanation: Diameter appears on both sides of the design equation through the size factor and the stress concentration. A first estimate with typical Marin and concentration factors is refined until the answers converge.

questions.stem: A shaft carrying two gears is found to meet the fatigue factor of safety but the deflection at one gear and the slope at one of its deep-groove ball bearings are too large. Describe the consequences of excessive deflection and slope, explain which design changes would reduce them and why changing to a higher-strength steel does not help.
markingGuide: Consequences: gear teeth mesh with misalignment, giving edge loading, noise, uneven wear and premature tooth failure; bearing elements run skewed, increasing contact stress and reducing life.
Deflection and slope are governed by $EI$ with $I=\pi d^4/64$, and by the span and load placement.

Changes: increase the diameter (deflection varies as $d^{-4}$), shorten the span or move bearings close to the gears, add an intermediate support, or change the arrangement of the gears to reduce moments.
Higher strength does not help because the modulus $E$ is practically the same for all steels (about 207 GPa), so stiffness is unchanged.
Alternatively use self-aligning or tapered bearings that tolerate larger slope, but gear alignment still needs control.
questions.explanation: Stiffness depends on geometry and the elastic modulus, not on strength. Only changing the geometry or support arrangement achieves a substantial improvement.
